introduction.heading: Why Test?
introduction.description: Automated tests are code that checks your code. Instead of manually clicking through an app after every change to see if it still works, a test suite does it in seconds - catching regressions before they reach a user, and giving you the confidence to refactor without fear.

concepts.title: Unit Test
concepts.description: Checks one small piece of code - usually a single function - in complete isolation

concepts.title: Integration Test
concepts.description: Checks that several real units work together correctly

concepts.title: Component Test
concepts.description: Renders one UI component and asserts on what it shows or does

concepts.title: Mocks & Spies
concepts.description: Test doubles - a mock replaces a dependency, a spy wraps the real one while recording calls

concepts.title: Fixture
concepts.description: Reusable, known-good sample data shared across tests

concepts.title: Assertion
concepts.description: The actual check, like expect(value).toBe(expected), that makes a test pass or fail

pyramid.heading: The Testing Pyramid
pyramid.description: Not every test should be the same kind. The testing pyramid is a guideline for how many of each kind to write: many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, and progressively fewer, slower tests as you move up toward exercising the whole app.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Pick a test runner and assertion library (Jest, Vitest, and Mocha + Chai are common choices)
Write small unit tests first, one behavior per test, following an Arrange-Act-Assert structure
Use mocks and spies to isolate the code under test from slow or unpredictable dependencies
Add integration and component tests for the seams unit tests can't reach on their own
Run the suite on every commit in CI so regressions get caught immediately, not in production

fullExample.heading: Test-Driven Development, Step by Step
fullExample.title: Red, green, refactor
fullExample.description: TDD flips the usual order: write a failing test that describes the behavior you want, write just enough code to pass it, then improve the implementation while the test keeps you honest. Click through the cycle below.

steps.label: Red - write a failing test
steps.explanation: With no formatPrice function yet, this test can't pass - it fails immediately. That's the point: it's a precise, executable description of the behavior you want, written before any implementation exists.

steps.label: Green - make it pass, minimally
steps.explanation: The smallest implementation that satisfies the test, and nothing more. It's tempting to add validation or extra formatting here, but TDD says: wait until a test asks for it.

steps.label: Add a test for a missing case
steps.explanation: A new requirement - reject non-numeric input - starts the cycle again. Writing this test first forces you to decide what 'reject' should mean (throw a TypeError) before you implement it.

steps.label: Refactor - clarify the implementation
steps.explanation: The old code happened to throw on non-numeric input too, but only because of an unrelated, confusing built-in error. This refactor makes the contract explicit and intentional - and because the existing tests still pass, you know the visible behavior hasn't changed.
